crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Vendor surveys show AI use is now the norm in life sciences, but they measure sentiment, not results.

Two 2025 surveys carry the claim. NVIDIA's healthcare and life sciences survey found 83 percent of respondents agreeing AI will revolutionise the field within three to five years. Salesforce found nearly all life sciences leaders expect AI agents to become essential within two years. Both point the same direction: adoption and expectation are high across the sector.

The pattern is enthusiasm measured at the level of intention. That is a weak signal for anyone deciding where compute, headcount or building capacity should go, because intention does not consume power and does not fill a data centre. The surveys say nothing about how much compute these organisations actually run, what they spend on it, or whether the workloads are production or pilot. For a sector whose AI ambitions ultimately rest on power and buildings, that is the missing number.

The data covers two vendor surveys and their headline findings. It does not cover sample sizes, response rates, or how either vendor defined AI use, and both vendors sell into the market they surveyed. Treat the figures as direction of travel. Judge your own programme on measured outcomes: time saved, quality, and cost per task.

explainer:
Surveys from technology vendors, consultancies and industry groups regularly report high and rising AI adoption in health care and life sciences, along with strong expectations for agents and generative AI. They are useful for spotting trends and common priorities.

They also have limits. Many are run by companies that sell AI, samples are often self selected, questions measure intentions and perceptions rather than results, and definitions of use vary. Treat survey figures as indicators of sentiment and direction, and judge your own programme on measured outcomes.

How to read adoption surveys

Surveys of AI adoption in life sciences arrive every few months from consultancies, vendors and industry bodies, and the headline numbers rarely agree. The differences come from who was asked and what counted. A survey of executives at large companies will report high adoption, because nearly every large company has a pilot. A survey asking whether AI is used in a validated production process will report far lower numbers. Neither is wrong; they measure different things.

The questions that make a survey useful

Who answered, and how many? Was the sample drawn by the sponsor from its own customers? What definition of adoption was used: experimenting, piloting, deployed in one function, or embedded in a regulated process? Did the survey separate research, clinical, manufacturing and commercial uses, which adopt at very different speeds? And did it ask about outcomes, such as time saved or decisions changed, rather than only intentions? Surveys that answer those questions are worth citing; the rest are marketing.

What the credible surveys agree on

Across the better studies, a few patterns hold. Commercial and medical writing functions adopt fastest because the risk is low and the time savings are visible. Manufacturing and pharmacovigilance adopt slowest because validation and inspection raise the cost of change. The gap between companies that have a governance framework and those that do not is widening, with the former moving pilots into production and the latter accumulating pilots that never scale. Data readiness, not model quality, is the most cited obstacle.
